Vertical urban farming

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
.......a farm where they farm without soil or sunlight and uses 95% less water than regular farms

Unique Selling Point:
A unique concept in farming -- using 95% less water than regular farms, no soil, no sunlight, no herbicides, pesticides of fungicides.

Summary:
A company aimed at sustainable farming and water preservation has developed technology that take aeroponics to a whole new level. They farm in abandoned warehouses in industrial parts of cities using stacks of trays under LED lights. They farm without soil or sunlight, and use 95% less water than ordinary farming. Their yield per square metre is 130 times that of regular farms and the harvest every 16 days, instead of every 60 days. They also use no pesticides, herbicides or fungicides.

Further information:
PROFITS FROM ECO-FRIENDLY VERTICAL FARMING STACK UP
NEWARK, NEW JERSEY —
Vertical farming — a tech-savvy subset of farming in which plants are stacked indoors, floor-to-ceiling, using controlled-environment agriculture (CEA) methods — is growing rapidly, changing the business landscape of traditional supply chains and growing seasons.
It is also having a profound effect on the environment.
Ask Newark, New Jersey-based AeroFarms, which set up shop in a neon-sprayed former paintball and laser tag arena next to a highway in the city’s Ironbound district. Its warehouse is the size of a Walmart Supercenter, but exclusively for leafy greens and herbs — more than 250 varieties.
AeroFarms aisles rise tall — accessible only by forklift crane — with shelves that are specialized growing labs using patented LED lights, aeroponic mist and reusable cloth.
To enter, farmers must suit up appropriately: gloves, lab coat, hairnet. Shoes must be disinfected.
AeroFarms’ high-yielding, economically efficient technology has made it the commercial leader in indoor farming, a market that is expected to quadruple over the next five years to nearly $4 billion.
AeroFarms co-founder and CEO David Rosenberg says the decision to focus on leafy greens was not based on any technological constraint, but rather business optimization.
“These are relatively high price-per-pound items, so it absorbs some of the price premiums with the new technology,” Rosenberg said.
AeroFarms’ output is consistent year-round, and it's consistently good for the environment — the effects of soil erosion, pesticides, water overuse and carbon emissions are heavily reduced, in some cases eliminated. The result is a net win for AeroFarms and the Earth.
“We could take up seed, we could grow it using 95 percent less water. In about 16 days our output per square foot is approximately 80 times per square foot over a field farmer, and we also grow using about 50 percent less fertilizers and zero pesticides, herbicides, fungicides,” Rosenberg said. “We could do this whether it is in the Sahara or a city like Newark.”
With indoor farms already in development on four continents, AeroFarms co-founder and chief marketing officer Marc Oshima says the company’s goals are to increase its production efficiency and scale operations worldwide near major distribution channels.
“We look at every single major urban environment as an opportunity,” Oshima said. “We look at things like urban density, we think about population, we think about people who are eating leafy greens.”

They also consider plants that are specific to their audience.
“We think about amaranth, one of the most popular greens in Africa and Southeast Asia. We think about how we can really bring and celebrate different types of varieties and different types of greens that are going to be specific to those regions.”
The farms also serve as tasting labs for AeroFarms' packaged varieties of supermarket-available, ready-to-eat leafy greens. Its baby watercress — labeled as “bright and crisp with a slight sweetness and a healthy dose of spice" — also happens to be an AeroFarms office favorite.
Alina Zolotareva, registered dietitian nutritionist and self-described foodie at AeroFarms, says her objective, from a public health standpoint, is to get people to eat more leafy greens like kale, one of the most nutritionally dense foods on the planet. To achieve this, producing the perfect taste is essential.
“Americans especially don't eat enough vegetables, so for me the most exciting part is all of the different flavors that we have here,” Zolotareva said. “It makes eating your vegetables so much more exciting and so much more fun.”
The farm’s specialty kale, in her opinion, “melts in your mouth.”
“A lot of people like the nutritional density of kale, but they don’t like the taste,” added Rosenberg. “So we can make a sweeter kale using the same seed, just stressing a plant to change the phytochemistry to get certain outcomes.”
Rosenberg says AeroFarms’ focus on leafy greens serves a greater function in addressing a growing food shortage worldwide. As part of a multifaceted approach to the crisis, he says consumers must shift their focus from calorie intake to nutrition.
Recent studies by the World Bank predict that an estimated global population of 9 billion in 2050 will require at least 50 percent more food. To add to the crisis, climate change is projected to cut crop yields by more than 25 percent during that span, an effect that would disproportionately affect the world’s poorest citizens.
AeroFarms, for its part, is slated to increase production significantly in the United States, in addition to its global operations. Less than a kilometer from its 2,800-square-meter farm is the site of its new global headquarters, a 6,500-square-meter former steel mill — the largest indoor vertical farm worldwide based on annual growing capacity, with a harvest rate of up to 900,000 kilos.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
MODERN FARMING WITH REDUCED ENVIRONMENTAL COST
Controlled indoor farming without the use of pesticides, fungicides, herbicides or even soil is the new way of growing food. In New Jersey, USA, the company Aerofarms has transformed a former Newark steel plant into a 22 000 square meter high-tech environment for production of herbs and vegetables.
The farming takes place within an indoor highly controlled environment. The production method is called vertical farming because the plants are not arranged in long rows but stacked upwards, optimising the space available.
Aerofarms is one of the leading companies utilising this food production method. According to co-founder and chief executive David Rosenberg, the advantages to the environment are huge. For instance; high-tech indoor farms use 95 percent less water than conventional, commercial field farms and there is no harmful run-off into the environment.
This is how it works: The plants grow on a reusable cloth medium that anchors their roots and is misted with a blend of nutrients, water and oxygen. Because the production is indoors and controlled, no pesticides, fungicides or herbicides are needed. According to Rosenberg, the production method requires approximately 50 percent less fertilizers compared to conventional methods of commercial greens productions.
Since vertical farming of greens only uses one percent of the land compared to traditional methods, the production can be done in urban areas close to the consumers. This also means less transportation.
The crops grow throughout the year and the production is not vulnerable to seasons, bad weather or crises like droughts or floods. The plants also grow at higher speed. According to Rosenberg at Aerofarms, farms will reap up to 30 harvests of greens a year.
Continuous monitoring with sensors optimizes the plants’ environment and ensures the plants will reach their peak and flavor potential. At Aerofarms, cameras, sensors and algorithms are used to collect and analyze data.
Lighting is one the largest expenditures. At Aerofarms, their specially designed LED lights comprise 50 percent of the company’s capital expenditure. Farmers using the new production methods have discovered that a mix of red and blue light works best to optimize photosynthesis and also requires less energy than standard yellow light.
Aerofarms, founded in 2004, now grows and sells 20 different leafy greens, including kale, arugula and romaine lettuce.
The company’s mission is to set a new standard for controlled urban agriculture and “address the global food crisis by building and operating indoor farms in cities across the United States and around the world, fundamentally transforming the business of agriculture to enable local food production at scale”.
Benefits of vertical farming:
* Year-round production, high quality growth with higher yields
* Faster, 12–16 day crop cycles give 22–30 crop turns per year
* A closed-loop system that uses 95 percent less water than outdoor agriculture
* Reusable growing cloth medium
* No pesticides, herbicides, fungicides
* No harmful run-off into the environment
* Significantly lower transportation kilometers due to farm proximity to markets served
* Better food safety controls and standards

Environmental costs of agriculture:
* According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the greenhouse gas emissions from agriculture, forestry and fisheries have nearly doubled over the past 50 years and could increase an additional 30 percent by 2050
* Agriculture is responsible for 70 percent of total freshwater withdrawals, which mainly goes to irrigating fields. (source: FAO)
* Agriculture is the prime cause of loss of species and main source of nutrient overload in aquatic and marine systems and a large chemical polluter.
(source: World Economic Forum)

2017/01/18 2:12:00 PM GM AC WG viewed on server -VERTICAL GARDENING
We liked it a lot, lovely story and links etc – thanks Eugene.
Changes:
• The starting sitting shots of the two ‘farmers’ please change to the two of them rather doing something farming – related/ in their context farming action shot that looks nothing like traditional farming/farmers would and tell us that they are farmers etc…
• We need to know what the nutrients the plants get are – what is the growth medium made of?
• We’ve not been at all critical in this piece at all – we have accepted what they are telling us exactly it seems. What criticism is there? We need more balance .
• We need to know more about the nutrient content – how does it compare nutritionally to food grown in soil and sun
• The visuals feel very repetitive like we see the same thing a lot
• We want to see a visual of ‘misting the roots’ – do you have this process?
• The end felt abrupt – do you have more of a holistic comment to end?
• Take out Claire’s first link with the punnets of leaves we felt wasn’t needed
• You need to come in at 8 mins please no longer – seems to be 08:50 long?
• Please send me your script to check
• Can you send us a link to watch it when you have made the changes? Wynand and I will view it no need for GM to see it, so just let us know when its ready.

Press Release:


Vertical Gardening
How does a unique vertical form of farming in industrial city blocks under LED lights achieve bumper yields without pesticides, soil or sunlight and using minimal water? Carte Blanche explores remarkable new technology taking aeroponic farming to new levels.


Script:


David:
I am a farmer and I want to change the world. On my farm we grow without sun, soil or pesticides.
V/O:
And this is David Rosenberg’s farm. One of the most sophisticated vertical indoor farms in the world. Here he farms with partner Marc Oshima in a warehouse in the industrial area of Newark, New Jersey. And they have taken farming to a whole new level.
13



Marc:
So here at Aerofarms we are thinking of indoor farming without sun or soil. We use aeroponics which is a form of hydroponics.
V/O:
Hydroponics is a method of growing plants without soil by bathing their roots in a nutrient rich liquid.
6
LINK:
Hydroponics has been around for some time, but uses a huge quantity of water and electricity. David and Marc’s approach is different and requires very little water.
9
Marc:
We are using water to deliver the nutrients but it is much more targeted than this hydroponics. So, here we have misting the roots as opposed to bathing the roots. So we can be much more sufficient, less water use, less nutrients, less fertilizers.
David:
We can grow a plant using 95% less water and 130 times the output per square foot over a traditional farm, meaning if a traditional farm can produce one pound, one kilo of product in a certain space, we can produce a 130 times that amount.
LINK:
Both Marc and David are passionate about the environment and the optimal use of water as resource is of paramount importance to them.
7

V/O:
In a world fast running out of water, they feel new approaches in agriculture are necessary.
6
David:
We are excited at Aerofarms at how we are changing and impacting the world. Agriculture has a lot of insufficiencies in the industry. Sixty percent of the world's water goes to agriculture, about sixty percent of the world's fresh water is polluted from agriculture. So, if one wants to solve water, look to agriculture.
V/O:
David and Marc met years ago when they were both national fencers, and decided to look at alternative ways of faming. David is also involved in major environmental organizations.
11
David:
I co-chair the circular economy taskforce for the World Economic Forum. Known for its meeting in Davos. I'm also a member of the B20 that advises the G20 in resource efficiency.
LINK:
David and Mark were able to put a dream team together to further their vision of changing the world. And what they have come up with is absolutely unique.
11
Marc:
We actually grow on cloth and so we have developed patterns around what is the correct weave and weft and what is the right porosity of that cloth. What the cloth provides us is a tremendous amount of advantages. We can grow a wide range of different crops. For leafy greens, we have grown over 250 different types of leafy greens and herbs.
V/O:
The cloth is porous and stretchable and each made from a 160 recycled plastic bottles. It is their own patent and not available commercially. Seeds are then sown on the cloth and watered. The trays are then treated with a growth medium, a process we were not allowed to film.

Once the seeds germinate, they are taken to 4 meter high stacks.

Then the trays with the seedlings are positioned under special LED lights. The trays hang above closed loop containers. The roots develop below the cloth and the leaves above the cloth.
19



7



13

Marc:
The cloth also serves as a barrier. So we are misting the roots underneath. Nothing ever touches the leaves. So again it is a clean, ready to eat product.
V/O:
The roots are misted with a solution containing all the nutrients plants naturally absorb from the soil.
7
LINK:
And farming without sunlight also has advantages.
3
Marc:
So we are able to grow without soil or sun. An idea that plants don't need sunlight, they need spectrum of light. And so it's our understanding of the biology, the plant science, really understanding how to have more effective photosynthesis indoors and be able to do it all year round.
David:
Our R&D team puts a lot of care and attention to what spectrum optimize photosynthesis and what spectrum doesn't. And we can eliminate other's that not wanted by the plants and greatly reduce our energy footprint.
V/O:
Their research has shown that if they change the frequency of the light it also has an effect on the plants. Here plants are subjected to a more blue-red spectrum.
12
Marc:
We can change the plant’s shape, the colour, nutrition and even flavour by using light and our nutrition in what we call our overall growing algorithm to be able to impact that. Again with the right mixture of red light, blue light we can change and create different characteristics. We can make something more red, we can create more anti-oxidants, we can make more flavour profiles.
LINK:
And by slight changes to the environment they are able to manipulate other characteristics of the crops as well.
7
David:
The same way we could stress a plant, changing its sleeping habits, eating habits, exercise habits to a certain extent, and change not their bio-chemistry but their phyto-chemistry. Their taste, their textures. Their nutritional densities, their colour, their yield.
Marc:
So we can make our arugula more peppery, we can make our mustard green more spicy, we can make our romaine lettuce more sweet.
LINK:
They can do all of this because they have a specialized team that monitors every aspect of the farm second by second.
Marc:
It is not one discipline. We have our plant scientists, the horticulture team, plant pathologists, crop physiologists. We have people on engineering: mechanical engineers, electrical engineers, structural engineers, industrial engineers, PLC engineers. We have micro-biologists on staff to ensure the right kind of food safety. We have nutritionists on staff.
V/O:
With this approach they are able to create crops that are exactly the same as field-grown plants. The only difference is that they are able to do it consistently every time.
Marc:
So this is a new way of farming if we think of the biology of the environment, if we think about the data-science and putting it all together. This is how we transform agriculture and that is our focus.
8
David:
It is fully controlled agriculture. It's an extremely exciting place to be and the average farm that we are building now , we are taking approximately 24 milion data points a day. We take those data plants that makes us smarter farmers with a better understanding of how plants work.
LINK:
Because they can create a consistent growing environment that is not subject to weather changes, the plants grow 3 times faster than on outdoor farms. They can harvest throughout the year.
12
V/O:
They don’t use pesticides, herbicides or fungicides. So when the plants are harvested, there is no need to wash them and the produce is immediately packaged and ready to eat.

No genetically modified seeds are used and because they can locate their farms in cities, their produce gets to shelves 4-5 days quicker than farm grown plants.

The facility we visited is in an old warehouse that once was used for paintball. Marc and David have left the inside as they found it. Their farms are deliberately constructed in challenged environments.
11


8


12

Marc:
We have growing that is going on in an inner city school right in their dining hall. We have growing that is going on in a former night club. We have growing on in a former steel mill. So we think about these different spaces and how we can have re-purpose them and revitalize communities.
V/O
So far they have built 8 farms and in this renovated Steel Mill in Newark they are installing the world’s biggest vertical farm that will produce hundreds of kilograms of fresh greens every day.
12
LINK:
Both Marc and David are driven and their water and space efficient farms in the USA are for them just the beginning. They have much bigger plans.
10
Marc:
So our mission is: how do we build responsible farms all over the world.

Carte Blanche explores remarkable new technology taking aeroponic farming to new levels. Script: David: I am a farmer and I want to change the world. On my farm we grow without sun, soil or pesticides. V/O: And this is David Rosenberg’s farm. One of the most sophisticated vertical indoor farms in the world. Here he farms with partner Marc Oshima in a warehouse in the industrial area of Newark, New Jersey. And they have taken farming to a whole new level. 13 Marc: So here at Aerofarms we are thinking of indoor farming without sun or soil. We use aeroponics which is a form of hydroponics. V/O: Hydroponics is a method of growing plants without soil by bathing their roots in a nutrient rich liquid. 6 LINK: Hydroponics has been around for some time, but uses a huge quantity of water and electricity. David and Marc’s approach is different and requires very little water. 9 Marc: We are using water to deliver the nutrients but it is much more targeted than this hydroponics. So, here we have misting the roots as opposed to bathing the roots. So we can be much more sufficient, less water use, less nutrients, less fertilizers. David: We can grow a plant using 95% less water and 130 times the output per square foot over a traditional farm, meaning if a traditional farm can produce one pound, one kilo of product in a certain space, we can produce a 130 times that amount. LINK: Both Marc and David are passionate about the environment and the optimal use of water as resource is of paramount importance to them. 7 V/O: In a world fast running out of water, they feel new approaches in agriculture are necessary. 6 David: We are excited at Aerofarms at how we are changing and impacting the world. Agriculture has a lot of insufficiencies in the industry. Sixty percent of the world's water goes to agriculture, about sixty percent of the world's fresh water is polluted from agriculture. So, if one wants to solve water, look to agriculture. V/O: David and Marc met years ago when they were both national fencers, and decided to look at alternative ways of faming. David is also involved in major environmental organizations. 11 David: I co-chair the circular economy taskforce for the World Economic Forum. Known for its meeting in Davos. I'm also a member of the B20 that advises the G20 in resource efficiency. LINK: David and Mark were able to put a dream team together to further their vision of changing the world. And what they have come up with is absolutely unique. 11 Marc: We actually grow on cloth and so we have developed patterns around what is the correct weave and weft and what is the right porosity of that cloth. What the cloth provides us is a tremendous amount of advantages. We can grow a wide range of different crops. For leafy greens, we have grown over 250 different types of leafy greens and herbs. V/O: The cloth is porous and stretchable and each made from a 160 recycled plastic bottles. It is their own patent and not available commercially. Seeds are then sown on the cloth and watered. The trays are then treated with a growth medium, a process we were not allowed to film. Once the seeds germinate, they are taken to 4 meter high stacks. Then the trays with the seedlings are positioned under special LED lights. The trays hang above closed loop containers. The roots develop below the cloth and the leaves above the cloth. 19 7 13 Marc: The cloth also serves as a barrier. So we are misting the roots underneath. Nothing ever touches the leaves. So again it is a clean, ready to eat product. V/O: The roots are misted with a solution containing all the nutrients plants naturally absorb from the soil. 7 LINK: And farming without sunlight also has advantages. 3 Marc: So we are able to grow without soil or sun. An idea that plants don't need sunlight, they need spectrum of light. And so it's our understanding of the biology, the plant science, really understanding how to have more effective photosynthesis indoors and be able to do it all year round. David: Our R&D team puts a lot of care and attention to what spectrum optimize photosynthesis and what spectrum doesn't. And we can eliminate other's that not wanted by the plants and greatly reduce our energy footprint. V/O: Their research has shown that if they change the frequency of the light it also has an effect on the plants. Here plants are subjected to a more blue-red spectrum. 12 Marc: We can change the plant’s shape, the colour, nutrition and even flavour by using light and our nutrition in what we call our overall growing algorithm to be able to impact that. Again with the right mixture of red light, blue light we can change and create different characteristics. We can make something more red, we can create more anti-oxidants, we can make more flavour profiles. LINK: And by slight changes to the environment they are able to manipulate other characteristics of the crops as well. 7 David: The same way we could stress a plant, changing its sleeping habits, eating habits, exercise habits to a certain extent, and change not their bio-chemistry but their phyto-chemistry. Their taste, their textures. Their nutritional densities, their colour, their yield. Marc: So we can make our arugula more peppery, we can make our mustard green more spicy, we can make our romaine lettuce more sweet. LINK: They can do all of this because they have a specialized team that monitors every aspect of the farm second by second. Marc: It is not one discipline. We have our plant scientists, the horticulture team, plant pathologists, crop physiologists. We have people on engineering: mechanical engineers, electrical engineers, structural engineers, industrial engineers, PLC engineers. We have micro-biologists on staff to ensure the right kind of food safety. We have nutritionists on staff. V/O: With this approach they are able to create crops that are exactly the same as field-grown plants. The only difference is that they are able to do it consistently every time. Marc: So this is a new way of farming if we think of the biology of the environment, if we think about the data-science and putting it all together. This is how we transform agriculture and that is our focus. 8 David: It is fully controlled agriculture. It's an extremely exciting place to be and the average farm that we are building now , we are taking approximately 24 milion data points a day. We take those data plants that makes us smarter farmers with a better understanding of how plants work. LINK: Because they can create a consistent growing environment that is not subject to weather changes, the plants grow 3 times faster than on outdoor farms. They can harvest throughout the year. 12 V/O: They don’t use pesticides, herbicides or fungicides. So when the plants are harvested, there is no need to wash them and the produce is immediately packaged and ready to eat. No genetically modified seeds are used and because they can locate their farms in cities, their produce gets to shelves 4-5 days quicker than farm grown plants. The facility we visited is in an old warehouse that once was used for paintball. Marc and David have left the inside as they found it. Their farms are deliberately constructed in challenged environments. 11 8 12 Marc: We have growing that is going on in an inner city school right in their dining hall. We have growing that is going on in a former night club. We have growing on in a former steel mill. So we think about these different spaces and how we can have re-purpose them and revitalize communities. V/O So far they have built 8 farms and in this renovated Steel Mill in Newark they are installing the world’s biggest vertical farm that will produce hundreds of kilograms of fresh greens every day. 12 LINK: Both Marc and David are driven and their water and space efficient farms in the USA are for them just the beginning. They have much bigger plans. 10 Marc: So our mission is: how do we build responsible farms all over the world.

metadata.Summary: A company aimed at sustainable farming and water preservation has developed technology that take aeroponics to a whole new level. They farm in abandoned warehouses in industrial parts of cities using stacks of trays under LED lights. They farm without soil or sunlight, and use 95% less water than ordinary farming. Their yield per square metre is 130 times that of regular farms and the harvest every 16 days, instead of every 60 days. They also use no pesticides, herbicides or fungicides.
metadata.Further information: PROFITS FROM ECO-FRIENDLY VERTICAL FARMING STACK UP NEWARK, NEW JERSEY — Vertical farming — a tech-savvy subset of farming in which plants are stacked indoors, floor-to-ceiling, using controlled-environment agriculture (CEA) methods — is growing rapidly, changing the business landscape of traditional supply chains and growing seasons. It is also having a profound effect on the environment. Ask Newark, New Jersey-based AeroFarms, which set up shop in a neon-sprayed former paintball and laser tag arena next to a highway in the city’s Ironbound district. Its warehouse is the size of a Walmart Supercenter, but exclusively for leafy greens and herbs — more than 250 varieties. AeroFarms aisles rise tall — accessible only by forklift crane — with shelves that are specialized growing labs using patented LED lights, aeroponic mist and reusable cloth. To enter, farmers must suit up appropriately: gloves, lab coat, hairnet. Shoes must be disinfected. AeroFarms’ high-yielding, economically efficient technology has made it the commercial leader in indoor farming, a market that is expected to quadruple over the next five years to nearly $4 billion. AeroFarms co-founder and CEO David Rosenberg says the decision to focus on leafy greens was not based on any technological constraint, but rather business optimization. “These are relatively high price-per-pound items, so it absorbs some of the price premiums with the new technology,” Rosenberg said. AeroFarms’ output is consistent year-round, and it's consistently good for the environment — the effects of soil erosion, pesticides, water overuse and carbon emissions are heavily reduced, in some cases eliminated. The result is a net win for AeroFarms and the Earth. “We could take up seed, we could grow it using 95 percent less water. In about 16 days our output per square foot is approximately 80 times per square foot over a field farmer, and we also grow using about 50 percent less fertilizers and zero pesticides, herbicides, fungicides,” Rosenberg said. “We could do this whether it is in the Sahara or a city like Newark.” With indoor farms already in development on four continents, AeroFarms co-founder and chief marketing officer Marc Oshima says the company’s goals are to increase its production efficiency and scale operations worldwide near major distribution channels. “We look at every single major urban environment as an opportunity,” Oshima said. “We look at things like urban density, we think about population, we think about people who are eating leafy greens.” They also consider plants that are specific to their audience. “We think about amaranth, one of the most popular greens in Africa and Southeast Asia. We think about how we can really bring and celebrate different types of varieties and different types of greens that are going to be specific to those regions.” The farms also serve as tasting labs for AeroFarms' packaged varieties of supermarket-available, ready-to-eat leafy greens. Its baby watercress — labeled as “bright and crisp with a slight sweetness and a healthy dose of spice" — also happens to be an AeroFarms office favorite. Alina Zolotareva, registered dietitian nutritionist and self-described foodie at AeroFarms, says her objective, from a public health standpoint, is to get people to eat more leafy greens like kale, one of the most nutritionally dense foods on the planet. To achieve this, producing the perfect taste is essential. “Americans especially don't eat enough vegetables, so for me the most exciting part is all of the different flavors that we have here,” Zolotareva said. “It makes eating your vegetables so much more exciting and so much more fun.” The farm’s specialty kale, in her opinion, “melts in your mouth.” “A lot of people like the nutritional density of kale, but they don’t like the taste,” added Rosenberg. “So we can make a sweeter kale using the same seed, just stressing a plant to change the phytochemistry to get certain outcomes.” Rosenberg says AeroFarms’ focus on leafy greens serves a greater function in addressing a growing food shortage worldwide. As part of a multifaceted approach to the crisis, he says consumers must shift their focus from calorie intake to nutrition. Recent studies by the World Bank predict that an estimated global population of 9 billion in 2050 will require at least 50 percent more food. To add to the crisis, climate change is projected to cut crop yields by more than 25 percent during that span, an effect that would disproportionately affect the world’s poorest citizens. AeroFarms, for its part, is slated to increase production significantly in the United States, in addition to its global operations. Less than a kilometer from its 2,800-square-meter farm is the site of its new global headquarters, a 6,500-square-meter former steel mill — the largest indoor vertical farm worldwide based on annual growing capacity, with a harvest rate of up to 900,000 kilos. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- MODERN FARMING WITH REDUCED ENVIRONMENTAL COST Controlled indoor farming without the use of pesticides, fungicides, herbicides or even soil is the new way of growing food. In New Jersey, USA, the company Aerofarms has transformed a former Newark steel plant into a 22 000 square meter high-tech environment for production of herbs and vegetables. The farming takes place within an indoor highly controlled environment. The production method is called vertical farming because the plants are not arranged in long rows but stacked upwards, optimising the space available. Aerofarms is one of the leading companies utilising this food production method. According to co-founder and chief executive David Rosenberg, the advantages to the environment are huge. For instance; high-tech indoor farms use 95 percent less water than conventional, commercial field farms and there is no harmful run-off into the environment. This is how it works: The plants grow on a reusable cloth medium that anchors their roots and is misted with a blend of nutrients, water and oxygen. Because the production is indoors and controlled, no pesticides, fungicides or herbicides are needed. According to Rosenberg, the production method requires approximately 50 percent less fertilizers compared to conventional methods of commercial greens productions. Since vertical farming of greens only uses one percent of the land compared to traditional methods, the production can be done in urban areas close to the consumers. This also means less transportation. The crops grow throughout the year and the production is not vulnerable to seasons, bad weather or crises like droughts or floods. The plants also grow at higher speed. According to Rosenberg at Aerofarms, farms will reap up to 30 harvests of greens a year. Continuous monitoring with sensors optimizes the plants’ environment and ensures the plants will reach their peak and flavor potential. At Aerofarms, cameras, sensors and algorithms are used to collect and analyze data. Lighting is one the largest expenditures. At Aerofarms, their specially designed LED lights comprise 50 percent of the company’s capital expenditure. Farmers using the new production methods have discovered that a mix of red and blue light works best to optimize photosynthesis and also requires less energy than standard yellow light. Aerofarms, founded in 2004, now grows and sells 20 different leafy greens, including kale, arugula and romaine lettuce. The company’s mission is to set a new standard for controlled urban agriculture and “address the global food crisis by building and operating indoor farms in cities across the United States and around the world, fundamentally transforming the business of agriculture to enable local food production at scale”. Benefits of vertical farming: * Year-round production, high quality growth with higher yields * Faster, 12–16 day crop cycles give 22–30 crop turns per year * A closed-loop system that uses 95 percent less water than outdoor agriculture * Reusable growing cloth medium * No pesticides, herbicides, fungicides * No harmful run-off into the environment * Significantly lower transportation kilometers due to farm proximity to markets served * Better food safety controls and standards Environmental costs of agriculture: * According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the greenhouse gas emissions from agriculture, forestry and fisheries have nearly doubled over the past 50 years and could increase an additional 30 percent by 2050 * Agriculture is responsible for 70 percent of total freshwater withdrawals, which mainly goes to irrigating fields. (source: FAO) * Agriculture is the prime cause of loss of species and main source of nutrient overload in aquatic and marine systems and a large chemical polluter. (source: World Economic Forum)
